name: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
title: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
answer: In the early grades, most general AI tools are not made for young children, and several require adult educator accounts or parental consent before a student can be invited. The practical rule is that when a young child does use an AI tool, the school must be able to name the adult who set it up and the adult who is watching. The largest benefit and smallest risk in these years comes from teachers using AI for planning and communication tasks.

sections.body: This idea sets out who may actually use AI in preschool through second grade. Most general AI tools are not built for young children, so the question is not whether the technology is impressive but whether a child of that age should be in front of it at all. The chapter draws a clear line between teacher use and student use, because the two carry very different levels of risk. It solves a common confusion in schools, where a tool that works well for a teacher is assumed to be suitable for the children in the room. The answer it gives is that adult use is the default in these grades, and any child use needs a named adult behind it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In preschool through second grade, the working pattern is teacher facing. An early childhood teacher uses AI for tasks it handles well, such as writing short stories at a child's reading level, making picture schedules, drafting notes to families, and turning scattered observations into clear summaries. Saving time on that work returns minutes to the teacher on the floor with children, which the chapter calls the heart of the matter. Where a school does set up student access, the text describes tools that require educator accounts belonging to adults, or teacher invitations with parental consent for children under 13. The chapter does not split these practices by narrower grade bands within the preschool to second grade range.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The chapter's evidence label rests on guidance rather than classroom trials. It cites UNESCO's recommendation that 13 be the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI, attributed to Miao and Holmes, 2023. It also describes the account rules of specific tools, noting that ChatGPT for Teachers is designed for educators only and offers no student accounts, that MagicSchool requires educator accounts to belong to adults with students using it only through a school's own setup, and that Canva for Education lets teachers invite students but requires parental consent for those under 13. No study of learning outcomes in these grades is offered. The claim that teacher use carries the largest benefit and smallest risk is presented as the chapter's judgement, not as a measured result.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are age and supervision. A preschooler or first grader is years away from the age line UNESCO sets for independent conversations with generative AI, so independent student use is not the model in these grades. When a young child does use a tool, the school must be able to name both the adult who set it up and the adult who is watching, which keeps responsibility with people rather than with the software. Consent for children under 13 stays with parents where a tool requires it, and account rules stay with the adults who hold the accounts. The decisions about what a child may use, and under whose eyes, remain with the school and the family.
